verdict: OK to lend in Amritsar woollens and shawls, but only to working-capital-led, low-leverage units with verified order books; avoid capex-heavy or leveraged mills.
title: Amritsar woollen & shawl textiles: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A shawl unit buys wool and yarn, gets it spun, dyed and woven or embroidered, and sells finished pieces into winter and export demand.** Cash sits in yarn and finished-goods inventory and in receivables from traders and exporters, not in the machines. Rating methodology flags the weaving business as both fixed-capital and working-capital intensive, with working capital driven by inventory holding and receivables [8][10]. So when a proposal lands, check the inventory and receivable days first; if finished-goods stock is more than one season old, ask for the ageing and the discount at which it is being cleared.

## What has changed now
**Input and freight costs have risen sharply, and the rupee fall and West Asia conflict are named as the cause in Amritsar manufacturing [2].** That is local news from March 2026, so treat it as the current cost picture until the customer shows otherwise. Peer results split cleanly: Prakash Woollen's Q1FY27 revenue rose 45% but operating costs rose 50%, leaving an operating loss of ₹218.11 lakh, with profit coming only from a ₹648.05 lakh NHAI land compensation [4][5]. Iris Clothings, by contrast, posted Q2FY27 total income of ₹62.22 crores, up 40.3%, at a 15.2% EBITDA margin [6]. **The lesson: volume growth is not margin growth in this trade.**

## Where the growth is
**Punjab GST collections grew 9.7% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1% [D], and India-wide IIP for NIC 13 output is up 13.1% YoY [D].** Pursue units with confirmed buyer orders, own embroidery or design capability, and a domestic-plus-export mix. Avoid pure job-work units with one buyer and no design margin, and avoid anyone funding a new shed or loom line on borrowed money while costs are moving like this. Amritsar-specific data is thin; the local sources are a cost report [2] and a 2025 piece on the industry re-establishing itself [3], so lean on first principles and the peers above.

## How to grow safely
**Structure as cash credit against inventory and receivables, with a term loan only where the machine has a named buyer contract.** Take monthly stock and receivable statements, quarterly GST returns, and a yearly unit-level margin sheet. Covenant a minimum EBITDA margin and a maximum total debt to EBITDA; rating methodology ties low leverage directly to financial flexibility in a downturn [11]. Where TUFS subsidy applies, match tenure to the subsidy window rather than stretching it [11].

## Early warning signs
**Watch for inventory days stretching, receivable days crossing the customer's own past average, and margin falling while sales rise.** If a unit's operating cost grows faster than revenue for two quarters, as at Prakash Woollen [4], stop enhancement and ask for the buyer-wise order book. If GST turnover diverges from bank credits, ask for the sales register.
watch: Inventory days rise two months running -> freeze limit enhancement and inspect godown
Quarterly GST returns vs bank credits
GST turnover falls below bank credits -> ask for sales register and buyer confirmations
Operating cost grows faster than revenue for two quarters -> move to collateral-backed exposure only
Leverage rises above covenant -> seek promoter infusion or reduce limit
